pages.title: How to Breed
pages.text: Feed a $(l:zen_amphibia:getting_started/crickets)cricket$(/l) to two tamed adult frogs. Each one will enter love mode and seek the other out. Once they meet, the genetics of the offspring are determined by both parents — see $(l:zen_amphibia:genetics/dna_basics)DNA Basics$(/l) for how inheritance works.

A breeding goal is what you want your frog line to become. For example: bigger frogs, better $(l:zen_amphibia:resources/frog_slime)slime$(/l), faster growth, tougher frogs, or safer heat-loving frogs.

pages.title: Why Breed?
pages.text: Wild frogs are a starting point, not the finish line. A random frog may have one useful trait, but breeding is how you make that trait reliable. Frog Buckets show standout breeding targets so you can decide which frogs to keep.

Better lines pay off in survival: Slime Yield and Size improve $(l:zen_amphibia:resources/frog_slime)Frog Slime$(/l), Coloration helps choose genetic froglight palettes, Power and Hardiness improve combat frogs, and Quickness, Tongue Length, and Temperament make stronger worker frogports when Create is installed.

Start small. Pick one trait, breed frogs that carry it, hatch their $(l:zen_amphibia:genetics/frogspawn)frogspawn$(/l), and inspect the $(l:zen_amphibia:lifecycle/tadpoles)tadpoles$(/l) or adults. Keep the best children and try again.
Great frog lines take generations. That is normal. If every baby was perfect, breeding would be over too quickly and the pond would be much less interesting.

$(b)Happiness bonus:$() Two parents kept in a quality $(l:zen_amphibia:getting_started/terrarium)terrarium$(/l) have a chance to pass along a small upgrade when they breed. At full happiness, there is a 15% chance one random gene locus in the offspring gains an allele tier. A slow but steady improvement on top of normal inheritance.
Tip: keep notes or use names for important frogs. A plain-looking $(l:zen_amphibia:genetics/alleles_and_carriers)carrier$(/l) can be more valuable than a flashy frog with poor hidden alleles.
